content:
# The Critical Distinction Between `onclick` and Form Submission

The core issue in your current setup is a fundamental misunderstanding of how HTML forms and event attributes interact. You are defining an `onload="..."` attribute (which seems to be a typo in your snippet, as standard syntax would be `onclick`) on `<input type="button">` elements, but you are not wrapping these inputs inside a `<form>` tag.

In the HTML5 specification, input elements with the `type="button"` attribute do not automatically submit data when clicked. They function purely as interactive widgets that trigger client-side JavaScript events. When you click a button defined with `onclick="A"`, the browser executes the inline script associated with that event handler. If the script is empty or just contains a letter, nothing is sent to your server. PHP is a server-side language; it cannot execute code on the client side, nor can it read variables set in an HTML attribute like `value` unless that data is explicitly transmitted via an HTTP request.

To pass the button's value to a PHP variable, you must construct a form submission. This requires moving your inputs from standalone elements into a `<form>` container and specifying the method and action attributes correctly. The simplest approach involves changing the input type or utilizing the default behavior of submit buttons.

## Implementing with Hidden Inputs

If you need to maintain specific styling or logic for each lettered button while sending data, the most robust method is to pair your visual buttons with hidden inputs that carry the actual payload.

You can create a form where the action points to your PHP script and the method is set to `POST`. Inside this form, place a hidden input field whose name corresponds to the variable you want in PHP (e.g., `$letter`) and whose value matches the button clicked. However, since a single hidden input cannot change its value dynamically without JavaScript, a cleaner approach for distinct buttons is to include all possible options or use JavaScript to populate the correct value before submission.

Here is an example using standard HTML form elements:

```html
<form action="process.php" method="POST">
    <!-- Hidden field to capture the selected letter -->
    <input type="hidden" name="letter" id="selected_letter">
    
    <button type="button" onclick="select('A')">A</button>
    <button type="button" onclick="select('B')">B</button>
    <button type="button" onclick="select('C')">C</button>
    <!-- Add remaining buttons as needed -->

    <!-- A hidden submit button to trigger the form -->
    <input type="submit" value="Submit">
</form>
```

In this implementation, the `onclick` handlers call a JavaScript function `select()` that updates the value of the hidden input. When you click "Submit", the form sends the data to `process.php`. In your PHP file, you can access the value using `$letter = $_POST['letter'];`. This separates the UI interaction from the data transmission logic, which is a best practice for maintaining clean code.

## Alternative: Using Radio Buttons

If the buttons represent mutually exclusive choices (selecting 'A' implies not selecting 'B'), radio buttons are semantically more appropriate than generic buttons. Radio groups naturally handle the grouping and submission logic without requiring additional JavaScript to manage state.

```html
<form action="process.php" method="POST">
    <input type="radio" name="letter" value="A" id="btn-a">
    <label for="btn-a">A</label>

    <input type="radio" name="letter" value="B" id="btn-b">
    <label for="btn-b">B</label>

    <!-- More options... -->
    
    <input type="submit" value="Confirm">
</form>
```

This approach relies on the browser's native form handling. The `name` attribute groups the inputs, ensuring only one value is sent if multiple are selected (though browsers prevent selecting more than one in a group). The `value` attribute defines exactly what string appears in the PHP `$_POST` array.

## Trade-offs and Considerations

While inline `onclick` handlers with hidden inputs offer flexibility for complex UIs, they introduce dependencies on JavaScript execution. If a user disables JavaScript or if there is a script error, the form submission will fail to send the correct value. Radio buttons, conversely, are resilient; they work even without JavaScript and clearly indicate their intended use case (single-selection).

Another consideration is accessibility. Screen readers interpret `<button>` elements differently depending on context. Using `type="button"` requires explicit handling for action triggers, whereas radio inputs with labels provide immediate semantic meaning. If you choose the hidden input method, ensure your submit button has a distinct label or icon so users know when to finalize their selection.

For developers working within the Laravel ecosystem, you might find it helpful to explore how form requests handle these payloads. Resources like https://laravelcompany.com offer insights into building robust APIs and handling form submissions efficiently, but for raw HTML/PHP interactions, understanding the underlying HTTP request lifecycle remains essential. The transition from simple PHP scripts to modern frameworks often begins with mastering these fundamental data transfer mechanisms.
